newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets to reap rewards of oil price rise.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets to reap rewards of oil price rise.

text.p: Tensions in the Middle East have meant unforeseen riches for oil exporting emerging markets, as higher petroleum prices translated into fresh revenues for cash-strapped budgets, U.S. analysts said Monday.
Several oil exporters had placed modest assumptions of oil prices into their budget projections, and can now reap the rewards of their prudence.
"The continued strength of oil prices has strengthened the balance of payments prospects for oil-exporting emerging markets countries," Merrill Lynch said in a release.
Petroleum prices surged last week when the U.S. military launched missile strikes against Iraq in response to Baghdad's incursion into protected Kurdish zones in the north of Iraq.
The Iraqi move caused the United Nations to suspend a deal that would have allowed Iraq to sell oil for food and medicines, sending oil prices higher.
Merrill Lynch estimated that Venezuela, Nigeria and Algeria would benefit the most from the oil surge, while Mexico, Ecuador and Colombia would realize modest gains.

"It's softening the recession, it's softening the adjustment, and it's going to let them get back into positive GDP growth at a much faster pace," said Molano, projecting a return to growth by the fourth quarter of 1996.
Analysts estimated that as the price of oil rises one dollar per barrel, Venezuela gains between $600 million and $800 million in revenues for state coffers.
Last week, the average export price for Venezuela's basket of crude and oil products rose to $20.05 per barrel, far outpacing the country's revised budget calculations at $15.60.
A Venezuelan official said last week that for every dollar the oil price goes up, the government would direct $210 million to a foreign debt buyback fund.
"There is a very explicit linkage between the price of oil and the size of any potential buyback (Venezuela) might engage in later on," Santamaria said.

Venezuelan Brady bonds have risen 3.2 percent month to date, doubling the gains of overall emerging markets debt, according to the JP Morgan Composite Index. Ecuadorean and Nigerian paper also outstipped the average.
"Venezuelan Bradies are probably going to continue trending up and probably we're going to see stability in Venezuelan assets," Molano said.

Even if tensions in the Gulf ebbed and the United Nations permited the Iraqi oil-for-food exchange, analysts doubted petroleum prices, which have been on the rise all year, would drop so dramatically to dim the positive impact on exporters.
Oil exporters may also find themselves better situated for any market volatility that stems from increases in U.S. interest rates, Merrill Lynch said.

NYMEX October crude oil slipped Monday after failing to crack the $24 per barrel price level, but traders cited support at $23.45. Earlier Monday, IPE Brent crude slipped back to the day's low of $22.50 per barrel.

"What you see now is really icing on the cake in terms of oil prices," said Marco Santamaria, vice president at ING Barings. "At the margin, it's better for these countries to have higher oil prices than lower."

The countries that have privatized, or at least liberalized their oil sectors, seemed likely to benefit the the most from the price movements, said Walter Molano, director of Latin American economic research at SBC Warburg.
Venezuela, for instance relies heavily on its oil sector and has boosted production, so the windfall should ease the pain of reforms that began in April, Molano said.
